claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel possesses an as-manufactured native oxide or passive film.
The onset of corrosion-related degradation in chloride-rich environments is governed by the temperature-dependent stability of Q235 steel's native oxide layer.
At approximately 25°C, the native oxide remains compact and protective.
A dense and adherent native oxide limits ingress of corrosive species.
At approximately 70°C, the native oxide film becomes destabilized.
Elevated temperature increases ionic mobility and reaction kinetics in the corrosive system.
Increased ionic mobility and reaction kinetics compromise the stability of the native oxide layer.
Destabilization of the native oxide produces a porous or cracked surface layer.
Porosity or microcracking permits more rapid penetration of corrosive agents.
A porous or cracked oxide layer facilitates localized corrosion such as pitting.
Q235 samples exposed at approximately 70°C will have a significantly higher corrosion rate than samples exposed to the same corrosive solution at approximately 25°C.
Q235 samples exposed at approximately 70°C will exhibit more pronounced localized corrosion and pit formation than samples exposed at approximately 25°C.
Q235 samples exposed at approximately 70°C will exhibit greater corrosion-related degradation than an unexposed or benign-environment control.
The proposed controlled study holds corrosive-medium composition, exposure duration, initial oxide state, and mechanical stress constant while varying temperature between approximately 25°C and 70°C.
The proposed mechanism is intended to apply only where medium composition and temperature are controlled and chemical exposure and temperature are the principal variables.
Variation in initial oxide-film quality may affect the observed corrosion behavior.
Failure of elevated-temperature exposure to increase corrosion rate, pitting, or detectable oxide degradation relative to room-temperature exposure would falsify the proposed mechanism.
